Your bot has one stop, and it is called "send". https://t.co/tau9RpOhDI printed 42,000 launches in one day this June, about one every two seconds. He never tried to read them, he built a line they all have to walk, one job per stop. The chain is new coin → Jev gate → OpenAI dots → Claude Opus 5.5 → his thumb → buy.

Stop one is the gate. Jev checks how much the dev holds, how much the top 10 wallets own and whether the buys came in bundles, and most coins die right there. Stop two is three OpenAI dots that never sleep: they read the wallet history, the dev's past launches and which smart wallets got in, read-only, so they can look at everything and touch nothing. Stop three is Opus 5.5, which gets the thesis, thinks and gives a verdict in one sentence, sign or reject. Stop four is him: even after Opus signs, the buy waits for one tap on his phone. One gate says no, Opus says yes, he taps approve.

The honest part: four stops make the bot slow, and some coins run before his thumb gets there. He decided that missing a few runners is cheaper than buying one rug at full speed.

note_tweet.text:
Codex、dots、ChatGPTの開発者の皆様へ。
dotsが本当に便利で、もっといろいろなことを任せたいと思っています。一方で、AIによる操作が、相手のサイトやアプリで不審な自動アクセスとして制限されないか、気になっています。
既存のエージェント識別の仕組みに加えて、「利用者本人から、どの範囲の操作を任されているか」を相手側も確認できる、代理人認証のような仕組みを広げていただけないでしょうか。
相手側のルールも尊重しながら、安心して代行を任せられるようになると嬉しいです。

To the developers of Codex, dots, and ChatGPT:
dots is incredibly useful, and I’d love to entrust it with more tasks. At the same time, I’m concerned that AI-driven actions might be flagged or restricted as suspicious automated activity by the websites and apps it interacts with.
Building on existing agent identification mechanisms, could you expand support for a system that lets those websites and apps verify exactly which actions a user has authorized an AI agent to perform on their behalf?
I’d love to be able to delegate tasks with greater confidence, while respecting each website’s and app’s rule
@OpenAI
